title: Farming Up
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: By the middle of this century, about two thirds of the world's people are expected to live in cities, and feeding them will be one of the great challenges of the age. Conventional farming already uses around seventy per cent of the fresh water that people take from rivers and lakes, and it takes up land that is often far from the customers it serves. One proposed answer is to move farming into the city itself, by growing crops in layers, one above another, inside a building. The idea is known as vertical farming.

The principle is straightforward. Instead of soil, the plants grow in shallow trays containing a nutrient solution, which is a mixture of water and dissolved minerals; this method is called hydroponics. A pump moves the solution from a tank through pipes to the trays, and whatever the plants do not absorb flows back to the tank to be used again. Because there is no sunlight inside a sealed building, LED lights above each layer provide the energy the plants need. These can be adjusted to produce the colours of light that plants use most efficiently, so that none is wasted.

Supporters list several advantages. Since the water is recirculated, a vertical farm can use a small fraction of the water needed to grow the same crop in a field. The growing area is closed off from the outside world, so pests are rarely a problem and pesticides are unnecessary. Crops can be harvested every month of the year, whatever the weather outside, and a farm in the middle of a city can deliver lettuce to nearby shops within hours of picking, rather than days.

Hydroponics is not the only system in use. In an aeroponic farm, the roots hang in the air and are sprayed with a fine mist of nutrients, which uses even less water. Aquaponic farms combine plants with tanks of fish, whose waste provides the nutrients that the plants need; in return the plants clean the water for the fish. Callum Reid, who runs an aquaponic farm in a former warehouse, says that his customers like the fact that they can buy fresh fish and vegetables from a single source.

The most serious drawback is energy. Lighting is the largest single cost of a vertical farm, and the electricity bill can decide whether a business survives. Dr Priya Nair has calculated that a kilogram of lettuce grown under artificial light may need many times more electricity than one grown in a greenhouse using free sunshine. Unless the power comes from renewable sources, she warns, a vertical farm may actually produce more carbon dioxide per kilogram of food than the farms it is supposed to replace.

There are also limits to what can be grown. At present vertical farms are profitable only for crops that are light, quick to grow and valuable, such as salad leaves, herbs and some soft fruit. The staple foods that supply most of the world's calories, including wheat, rice and potatoes, are much too bulky and slow to be grown economically under lights. Several well-funded companies have closed after failing to cover their costs, and investors have become more careful as a result.

Nevertheless, the technology continues to improve. LED lights are becoming cheaper and more efficient, and machines now carry out much of the planting and harvesting that once required human workers. Most experts see vertical farming as a supplement to conventional agriculture and not a replacement for it. It may prove most useful in places where the alternatives are poor, such as desert cities with little rainfall, or research stations in Antarctica, where fresh food is otherwise impossible to obtain.

items.s: Conventional farming uses about seventy per cent of the fresh water taken from rivers and lakes.
e: around seventy per cent of the fresh water

items.s: Most farms are located close to the customers they serve.
e: often far from the customers it serves

items.s: Hydroponic plants grow in soil enriched with minerals.
e: Instead of soil, the plants grow in shallow trays

items.s: LED lights can be adjusted to give the colours that plants use best.
e: can be adjusted to produce the colours of light that plants use most efficiently

items.s: Vertical farms need strong pesticides to control insects.
Aeroponic farms use less water than hydroponic farms.
Aquaponic farms in Britain have been more successful than those elsewhere.
e: Callum Reid, who runs an aquaponic farm in a former warehouse
items.w: No comparison between countries is made.

items.s: Nair found that greenhouse lettuce needs more electricity than lettuce grown under lights.
e: may need many times more electricity than one grown in a greenhouse

items.s: Wheat can be grown profitably in vertical farms.
e: much too bulky and slow to be grown economically under lights

items.s: Some vertical farming companies have gone out of business.
Vertical farms are expected to replace conventional agriculture.
e: a supplement to conventional agriculture and not a replacement for it

items.q: Why is the solution in a hydroponic system returned to the tank?
o: It must be cooled before reuse.
The plants do not absorb all of it.
It has to be cleaned of fish waste.
The pump cannot move it upwards.
e: whatever the plants do not absorb flows back to the tank to be used again

items.q: What is the main reason why Dr Nair is concerned about vertical farms?
o: the amount of water they waste
the size of the buildings needed
e: The most serious drawback is energy

items.q: What does the writer suggest about the future of vertical farming?
o: It will mostly be useful in specialised places.
It will soon be cheaper than field farming.
It will become unnecessary as lights improve.
It will mainly grow staple crops.
e: It may prove most useful in places where the alternatives are poor

groups.qt: Which TWO advantages of vertical farms are mentioned in paragraph C?
o: The farms can produce crops throughout the year.
The crops can be grown without sunlight or electricity.
Fresh produce reaches shops very quickly.
The crops taste sweeter than field crops.
e: Crops can be harvested every month of the year
within hours of picking, rather than days

items.s: a prediction about where most people will live
e: about two thirds of the world's people are expected to live in cities

e: machines now carry out much of the planting and harvesting

e: produce more carbon dioxide per kilogram of food

items.s: examples of crops that are too bulky for vertical farms
A ___ moves the nutrient solution from the tank to the trays.
e: A pump moves the solution from a tank

items.s: Plants in vertical farms receive light from ___ above each layer.
Farms in cities can deliver lettuce to shops within ___ of picking.
In an aeroponic system the roots hang in the ___.
e: the roots hang in the air

items.s: Lighting is the largest single ___ of a vertical farm.
e: Lighting is the largest single cost

items.s: Vertical farms are profitable at present only for crops that are valuable, light and ___ to grow.
e: light, quick to grow and valuable

items.q: What do hydroponic plants grow in instead of soil?
e: shallow trays containing a nutrient solution

items.q: What does fish waste provide for the plants in an aquaponic farm?
e: provides the nutrients that the plants need

items.q: Which kind of building did Callum Reid's farm replace?
Where might a vertical farm provide fresh food in a place with no other sources?
